title: My colony sim RPG uses a built-in language model, which lets you ask NPCs anything, convince them to take actions, and bargain with the gods
author: epochforgegame
selftext:
Hey! My game's full demo is coming out on the 18th[ (Epoch Forge - feel free to wishlist!)](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5062230/Epoch_Forge/) and I'm very excited to talk about the way it uses GenAI. 

A little background. I got the idea from playing mods like Mantella in Fallout, CHIM in Skyrim, and random ones that hooked into Rimworld, Bannerlord, etc. as well as training my own models for mod making. The thing I realized is that none of the mods adding an LLM to the game actually *did* much. Talking to NPCs was fun, but the most depth you'd get is that NPC giving you an attitude next time you talk. So I decided to make a game that does it myself.

It's a sidescroller with a massive open world, handmade blueprints for every structure, faithful retro graphics and sounds, and realistic physics + events within that world.

I've spent many months refining it and testing it on my own PCs, and the current system works like this:

* The game auto-detects your available compute resources. Then, it chooses either a Gemma E2B model, or an E4B model (you can also choose manually). You can also BYOK or point to a local model of your choice, it works with just about anything, even low-tier free models. 
* A llama server starts with the game, running the model. If you set your own, this doesn't happen. 
* Every NPC in the game has an in-depth prompt. It describes things like:
   * Their name
   * Their traits - mistrusting, charitable, isolated, sociable, etc.
   * Their race, appearance, location, living status and work
   * What they can see of the player - so they will recognize what they know visually, but they don't automatically know your entire personality like that thing from Deus Ex. 
   * The most exciting part by far - what I call the Oracle system. A vast majority of the work has gone into this part, and I genuinely think it's one of a kind. Basically, there is a knowledge domain for every topic an in-world NPC could know, and they are only told those things. So a Dwarven miner literally cannot access information about a famous Elf miles away or a ritual they don't practice. I've run thousands of looping tests and have not seen a single instance of hallucination yet. See attached GIF for a look into one character.
* The Storyteller. You can [read this post](https://fiddlesticksgaming.itch.io/epochforge/devlog/1699466/dev-log-9-your-game-is-run-by-an-omniscient-storyteller-that-builds-the-world-around-your-choices) or ask me directly if you want to know more about this, but basically, an all-knowing deity chooses all the random things that happen in your game. That part is procedural - the LLM lets you actually ask them things. You can plead for mercy and bargain them to call off a raid, in exchange for facing a stronger one a week from now. You can ask what led them to send a meteor strike at you. I'll edit this post later tonight with a clip of that happening. The whole system works with or without an LLM, but the LLM adds a lot of unique flavor.

Overall, I'm super excited about this project. It originated from genuine passion for this niche and I really believe it will be the first of its kind. Again, please [wishlist ](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5062230/Epoch_Forge/)if this sounds interesting! I'd also love feedback if you have any. Questions, suggestions, criticisms, etc. are all welcome. Thank you!

  
[If you'd like to watch a short clip of the system I have one here.](https://drive.google.com/file/d/11ykaMQNcsanVlbyEDzq4iKxkOzLdOaGH/view) It shows how an NPC knows of the residents of their city, remembers what you said, and how some are more likely than others to hold a grudge.

comments.author: SlightOfHand_
comments.body: I think there’s a lot of potential for systems like this in RPGs. It makes a lot of sense. So far I’ve only seen development like this towards pen and paper AI dungeon master programs, and those are always subscription services. Setting this up locally and letting people use their own models is really clutch.

replies.author: epochforgegame
replies.body: Thank you! I agree. My hope was to make it accessible for people that just want to download one thing rather than having to learn how to host an LLM/generate a key. It comes with the tradeoff that the model is pretty small and therefore not always perfect quality, but I'm excited to see people play the demo and test how it actually runs.

replies.author: MidSerpent
replies.body:
I’ve been building a small language model kernel specifically for this purpose, being fully under the control of the developer and game engine, inside the game engine not running on Llama.

Has a bunch of features targeted specifically for game developer needs, like schema constrained generation (output schemas can’t mathematically can’t be wrong)

V1.0 of the Unreal plugin is a little slow, but I’ve got some big speed ups coming.

Relevant to you is the feature I’m working on now, prefix-KV memory swapping. In other words, rather than reprocessing your long prefix, you can just swap it in from the disk. 

https://github.com/dansupergameprogrammer/SuperSLM

https://github.com/dansupergameprogrammer/SuperSLM-unreal

replies.author: Rikkendo
replies.body:
Since you mentioned pen&paper/RPGs, I am developing a game called Warrior Quest exactly like that without a subscription service.

It should feel like a solo d&d campaign.

It does not currently offer local models though but you can try out the [free demo](
https://store.steampowered.com/app/5120060/Warrior_Quest_Demo/
)

But hats off to OP, seems like he’s pioneering in a different way, I look forward to trying his game.
